strengthening-001.question: Estimating the shear stress needed to displace the atomic planes above and below the slip plane all at once in a perfect crystal (the theoretical shear strength) as τ ≈ G/2π gives about 7.6 GPa for copper (shear modulus G = 48 GPa). Which is the correct reason why the shear stress at which a real copper single crystal begins to slip is orders of magnitude smaller, about 1 MPa?
choices: When a dislocation in the crystal moves, bonds across the slip plane only need to be rearranged one row at a time, so the whole plane need not be displaced at once
Vacancies in the crystal diffuse and gather on the slip plane, and atomic planes separate all at once where vacancies are concentrated, reducing the number of bonds to break
The oxide film on the surface of the single crystal acts as a lubricant between atomic planes, so displacement begins at a force weaker than the internal bonds
strengthening-001.explanation: The theoretical shear strength assumes that all the atoms above and below the slip plane shift to the neighboring positions simultaneously; it is G/2π ≈ 7.6 GPa, and even with a more realistic form of the interatomic force it is about G/30, or about 1.6 GPa. Real yielding occurs at less than a thousandth of this because the crystal contains dislocations, and when a dislocation moves only the bonds at the dislocation line are rearranged in turn, so the displacement spreads a little at a time. Vacancy diffusion does not carry slip at room temperature; it is a mechanism that matters in high-temperature creep and similar processes. A surface oxide film, if anything, can hinder dislocations from leaving through the surface. Strengths close to the theoretical value have been measured in whiskers, which contain almost no dislocations.

strengthening-002.question: A single-crystal rod is pulled in tension. For a slip system whose slip-plane normal makes 60° and whose slip direction makes 40° with the tensile axis, the critical resolved shear stress is 0.80 MPa. Which is closest to the tensile stress at which this slip system begins to slip? Ignore other slip systems.
choices: About 0.31 MPa
About 1.6 MPa
About 2.1 MPa
strengthening-002.explanation: The resolved shear stress on a slip system is τ = σ cosφ cosλ (Schmid's law), and cosφ cosλ is called the Schmid factor. Here cos60° × cos40° = 0.500 × 0.766 ≈ 0.383, so slip begins at σ = 0.80/0.383 ≈ 2.1 MPa. About 0.31 MPa multiplies the critical resolved shear stress by the Schmid factor instead of dividing, and about 1.6 MPa divides only by cosφ and forgets cosλ. The Schmid factor reaches its maximum of 0.5 when the slip-plane normal and the slip direction both make 45° with the tensile axis, and it is 0 when the slip plane is parallel or perpendicular to the axis, in which case that system does not slip. In a single crystal, the system with the largest factor slips first.

strengthening-003.question: The yield stress σy of an FCC polycrystal is about three times the critical resolved shear stress τc of a single crystal (σy ≈ Mτc, M ≈ 3.06). Which is the correct reason why this factor M (the Taylor factor) is larger than 2, the reciprocal of the maximum Schmid factor of 0.5?
choices: In a polycrystal only the most favorably oriented grains slip first while the others stay elastic, so M becomes larger to make up for the lower average strength
For neighboring grains to deform without opening gaps or overlapping at the grain boundaries, at least five independent slip systems must operate in each grain, including poorly oriented ones
A polycrystal has far more grain-boundary area than a single crystal, and the grain-boundary energy adds to the work of deformation, so M is about 3 regardless of grain size
strengthening-003.explanation: In a polycrystal, if each grain deformed into any shape it liked, gaps and overlaps would open at the grain boundaries. To accommodate an arbitrary change of shape at constant volume, five independent slip systems are needed (the von Mises criterion). As a result, poorly oriented systems must operate along with those of high Schmid factor, and averaging over a randomly oriented FCC polycrystal gives a Taylor factor of about 3.06. If yielding were set only by the most favorably oriented grains, a factor larger than 2 could not be explained. The Taylor factor is set by the distribution of grain orientations and does not depend on grain-boundary area or grain size; the effect of grain size is added separately through the Hall–Petch relationship. The same criterion explains why polycrystals of HCP metals, which lack enough independent slip systems, have poor ductility.

strengthening-004.question: The yield stress of BCC metals such as iron rises sharply as the temperature is lowered, whereas in FCC metals such as copper and aluminum it changes little with temperature. Which is the main cause of this difference?
choices: In FCC metals the stacking-fault energy falls at low temperature and dislocations dissociate and move more easily, so the yield stress actually falls at low temperature
In BCC metals interstitial carbon and nitrogen gather more readily at dislocations at low temperature, so pinning by Cottrell atmospheres grows stronger as the temperature falls

The cores of screw dislocations in BCC metals spread over several planes and move with difficulty, overcoming the lattice resistance with the help of thermal fluctuations, so more stress is needed at lower temperature
strengthening-004.explanation: The cores of screw dislocations in BCC metals do not spread flat on a single plane but take a three-dimensional form extending over several {110} planes, so the Peierls stress, the resistance of the lattice to dislocation motion, is large. Dislocations cross this barrier a little at a time with the help of thermal fluctuations (formation of kink pairs), so as the temperature falls this help diminishes and the yield stress rises steeply. This is one reason for the ductile-to-brittle transition of BCC steels. Dislocations in FCC metals are dissociated flat on the close-packed planes, the Peierls stress is small and the yield stress depends little on temperature. The option in which the yield stress falls at low temperature contradicts the facts, and high-purity BCC metals free of carbon and nitrogen show the same temperature dependence, so the option attributing it mainly to Cottrell atmospheres is also wrong.

strengthening-005.question: In a substitutional solid solution, assume that the increase in yield stress Δσ is proportional to the square root of the solute concentration c (the Fleischer model). If Δσ = 30 MPa at 1 at% solute, which is closest to Δσ at 4 at% solute? Ignore interactions between solute atoms and precipitation.
choices: About 60 MPa
About 120 MPa
About 76 MPa
strengthening-005.explanation: Since Δσ ∝ c^(1/2), a fourfold increase in concentration doubles Δσ (√4 = 2), giving 30 × 2 = 60 MPa. About 120 MPa assumes that Δσ is proportional to concentration, and about 76 MPa uses the Labusch model, in which Δσ is proportional to concentration to the power 2/3 (30 × 4^(2/3) ≈ 76), which is not the premise of this question. The Fleischer model treats a dislocation as being caught one at a time on widely scattered solute atoms, and the resistance of each is set by the difference in atomic size between solute and matrix (the size effect) and the difference in shear modulus (the modulus effect). Because the gain in strength slows as the concentration increases, choosing elements with large size or modulus differences is what pays off when seeking high strength from solid-solution strengthening.

strengthening-006.question: When annealed low-carbon steel is pulled in tension, the stress drops after an upper yield point and a yield-point phenomenon appears in which Lüders bands travel along the specimen. Which statement about this phenomenon and its remedy is correct?
choices: It occurs because cementite precipitated at grain boundaries hinders the generation of dislocations, so dissolving the cementite by quenching keeps it from appearing even after months at room temperature
It occurs because carbon and nitrogen atoms gather at and pin dislocations; light cold rolling to add mobile dislocations removes it, but it can reappear if the steel is left at room temperature
The upper yield point arises from dislocations piling up at grain boundaries, so coarsening the grains to reduce the boundaries prevents both the yield-point phenomenon and Lüders bands
strengthening-006.explanation: In low-carbon steel, interstitial carbon and nitrogen atoms gather around dislocations (Cottrell atmospheres) and pin them. Yielding needs a large stress to tear dislocations away or create new ones (the upper yield point), and once they start moving deformation proceeds at a lower stress, so a deformed band travels along the specimen. Because this produces surface markings on pressed parts (stretcher strains), steel sheet is given about 1% temper rolling to add mobile dislocations before use. However, when dissolved carbon and nitrogen diffuse and pin the dislocations again, the yield point returns (strain aging); this does not happen in IF steel, where carbon and nitrogen are tied up as compounds by Ti or Nb. The options that explain it by cementite or by pile-ups at grain boundaries are wrong.

strengthening-007.question: The flow stress of a work-hardened metal is estimated with the Taylor equation σ = MαGb√ρ (ρ is the dislocation density). For cold-worked copper with M = 3.06, α = 0.3, G = 48 GPa, b = 0.256 nm and ρ = 1.0×10¹⁴ m⁻², which is closest to σ?
choices: About 37 MPa
About 376 MPa
About 113 MPa
strengthening-007.explanation: Since √ρ = 1.0×10⁷ m⁻¹, σ = 3.06 × 0.3 × 48×10⁹ × 0.256×10⁻⁹ × 1.0×10⁷ ≈ 1.13×10⁸ Pa, about 113 MPa. About 37 MPa is the resolved shear stress obtained by forgetting to multiply by the Taylor factor M, and about 376 MPa forgets the coefficient α. The Taylor equation comes from the fact that moving dislocations are caught where they intersect other dislocations (forest dislocations), whose spacing is of the order of 1/√ρ. The dislocation density of annealed metals is about 10¹⁰ to 10¹² m⁻², rising to about 10¹⁵ m⁻² after heavy cold work. A hundredfold increase in dislocation density raises the strength only tenfold, so work hardening gradually slows as the strain grows.

strengthening-008.question: When a metal is plastically deformed in tension, unloaded and then compressed in the reverse direction, the yield stress in compression is lower than the flow stress it would have had if tension had continued. Which is the correct explanation of this phenomenon (the Bauschinger effect)?
choices: Dislocations piled up against obstacles during tension leave an internal stress in the opposite direction (back stress), which assists deformation in the reverse direction
Vacancies created during tension gather into voids after unloading, and in compression the voids collapse, lowering the apparent yield stress
Plastic deformation in tension elongates the grains along the tensile direction and makes them finer, so that only the compressive yield stress falls through the Hall–Petch relationship
strengthening-008.explanation: During tension, dislocations pile up against grain boundaries, precipitates and clusters of other dislocations, and Orowan loops remain around hard particles. These create an internal stress (back stress) that opposes the tensile deformation and assists deformation in the reverse direction. So when the loading is reversed, the back stress acts to push the dislocations back, and compression begins at a lower stress. Gathering or collapse of vacancies cannot explain it. Grain refinement, through the Hall–Petch relationship, raises both the tensile and the compressive yield stress, so it cannot be why only the compressive one falls. The Bauschinger effect must be taken into account in analyzing members under cyclic loading, in reverse bending of sheet and in assessing the strength of formed steel pipe.

strengthening-009.question: As precipitates grow during aging, the strength rises to a maximum and then falls (overaging). Which is the correct explanation in terms of the interaction between precipitates and dislocations? Take the volume fraction of precipitates as constant.
choices: Small precipitates are bypassed by dislocations and larger ones come to be sheared, and the stress needed to shear them increases as the spacing between precipitates widens

Small precipitates are sheared by dislocations with a resistance that grows with their size, but larger ones are passed by dislocations bowing out between them, at a stress that falls as the spacing widens

Precipitates of every size are sheared, and as they grow their coherency with the matrix increases so the shearing resistance keeps rising, while the maximum strength is set by the loss of solid-solution strengthening
strengthening-009.explanation: The small, coherent precipitates of early aging are sheared and passed through by dislocations. The resistance to shearing comes from the work of creating coherency strain, new interface and, for ordered phases, an antiphase boundary, and at a constant volume fraction it increases as the precipitates grow. Once precipitates become large, it becomes easier for dislocations to bow out between them and pass, leaving loops (the Orowan mechanism), and that stress is inversely proportional to the precipitate spacing, so it falls as the particles coarsen. The strength peaks at the size where the two mechanisms change over, which corresponds to peak aging. The option with the order of bypassing and shearing reversed is wrong. Precipitates tend to lose coherency with the matrix as they grow, so the option in which coherency increases is also wrong.

strengthening-010.question: In an aluminum alloy, the increase in shear stress due to the Orowan mechanism, in which dislocations bow out and pass between precipitates, is estimated as Δτ ≈ Gb/L (L is the precipitate spacing). With G = 26 GPa, b = 0.286 nm and L = 100 nm, and taking the increase in the yield stress of the polycrystal as Δσ = MΔτ (Taylor factor M = 3.06), which is closest to Δσ?
choices: About 74 MPa
About 228 MPa
About 24 MPa
strengthening-010.explanation: Δτ = 26×10⁹ × 0.286×10⁻⁹/(100×10⁻⁹) ≈ 7.4×10⁷ Pa, about 74 MPa. Converting to the increase in the yield stress of a polycrystal means multiplying by the Taylor factor, Δσ = 3.06 × 74 ≈ 228 MPa. About 74 MPa leaves the value as a shear stress and forgets M, and about 24 MPa divides by M. The expression comes from the line tension of a dislocation, about Gb²/2, and the fact that a dislocation can pass once it has bowed out into a semicircle between precipitates. At the same volume fraction, finer particles have a smaller spacing L, so the Orowan stress is larger. More precise expressions include a factor for the dislocation character and particle size and a logarithmic term, which give values smaller than this estimate.

strengthening-011.question: Which statement about the characteristics of dislocations shearing through precipitates with an ordered structure, such as the γ' phase (an L1₂ ordered phase) in Ni-based superalloys, is correct?
choices: In an ordered phase the period of the atomic arrangement is half that of the matrix, so a matrix dislocation splits into two partial dislocations inside the precipitate with a twin between them
Ordered precipitates are incoherent with the matrix and are never sheared by dislocations, so dislocations bow out and pass between particles of every size
A single dislocation that cuts the precipitate leaves an antiphase boundary with the atomic arrangement out of step, so a second dislocation follows to remove it and dislocations move in pairs
strengthening-011.explanation: In an ordered phase, atoms of different kinds sit on specific sites. When a perfect dislocation of the FCC matrix, (a/2)<110>, cuts a precipitate, the pairing of atoms above and below the slip plane is shifted, creating an antiphase boundary (APB), and its energy is the resistance to shearing. In the ordered phase the original arrangement is restored only after a shift of a<110>, so a second dislocation with the same Burgers vector follows to remove the APB, and the dislocations move as a coupled pair, a superdislocation. The period of the ordered arrangement is longer than that of the matrix, not half of it. γ' is coherent with the matrix, so while small it is normally sheared, and the option claiming it is incoherent and never sheared is also wrong. Precipitating a large amount of γ' with a high APB energy is the key to the high-temperature strength of superalloys.

strengthening-012.question: Which statement about dispersion strengthening with oxide particles, as in copper containing fine Al₂O₃ particles or ODS steels with Y₂O₃ particles dispersed in iron, is correct?
choices: It uses coherent oxides precipitated from the matrix by aging, so the strength can be adjusted just as in precipitation hardening by choosing the solution-treatment and aging temperatures
Hard oxides that do not dissolve in the matrix and resist coarsening force dislocations to bypass them, so strength tends to remain even at high temperatures where precipitates dissolve or coarsen

It strengthens through the antiphase boundary created when dislocations shear the oxide particles, so larger particles give more strength, and at high temperature the particles dissolve and ductility returns
strengthening-012.explanation: In dispersion strengthening, oxide particles that hardly dissolve in or react with the matrix are produced and dispersed by internal oxidation or by mechanical alloying, in which powders are mixed intensely. Hard, incoherent particles are not sheared by dislocations and strengthen through the Orowan mechanism. Precipitates lose their strength at high temperature by dissolving or coarsening through Ostwald ripening, but oxide particles change little up to near the melting point, so strength and creep resistance at high temperature are retained. Al₂O₃-dispersed copper is used for welding electrodes and other parts that must resist softening at high temperature, and ODS steels are candidate materials for nuclear fuel cladding. The option about precipitating by aging describes precipitation hardening; oxides do not dissolve in the matrix, so they cannot be solution treated. Antiphase boundaries concern the shearing of ordered precipitates.

strengthening-013.question: The yield stress of an alloy is estimated from contributions of 50 MPa friction stress, 60 MPa solid-solution strengthening, 200 MPa precipitation strengthening and 100 MPa dislocation strengthening. If the friction stress and solid-solution strengthening are simply added, while the contributions of precipitates and dislocations, which are obstacles of similar strength, are combined as the square root of the sum of squares (σ = σ₀ + σss + √(σp² + σd²)), which is closest to the yield stress?
choices: About 334 MPa
About 410 MPa
About 237 MPa
strengthening-013.explanation: The precipitate and dislocation contributions combine to √(200² + 100²) = √50000 ≈ 224 MPa, and adding 50 + 60 = 110 MPa gives about 334 MPa. About 410 MPa is the simple sum of everything, and about 237 MPa combines everything as the root sum of squares. When point obstacles of similar strength are mixed on the same slip plane, a dislocation is caught on them without distinguishing between them, so the strength approaches the root sum of squares. Obstacles of very different strengths, or resistances of a different nature such as lattice friction, are closer to simple addition. Intermediate exponents are also used, and the choice of combination changes the estimate by tens of percent, so comparisons should state which expression was used.

strengthening-014.question: Which method of strengthening steel raises the yield strength while also lowering the ductile-to-brittle transition temperature, improving toughness at low temperatures?
choices: Work hardening by raising the dislocation density through cold work
Solid-solution strengthening by dissolved phosphorus or silicon
Grain refinement by controlled rolling and similar processes
strengthening-014.explanation: Refining the grains raises the yield strength through the Hall–Petch relationship and, because cleavage cracks change direction or stop at grain boundaries, it also raises the stress needed to initiate and propagate cracks, so the ductile-to-brittle transition temperature falls. In steel the Hall–Petch coefficient is about 0.6 to 0.7 MPa·√m, larger than in aluminum or copper, so refinement is especially effective, and thermomechanical controlled processing (TMCP), in which steel containing Nb or Ti is rolled at low temperature and then accelerated-cooled, is widely used to strengthen steels for welded structures. Work hardening, precipitation strengthening and solid-solution strengthening by most elements other than Ni raise the yield strength but tend to raise the transition temperature and lower toughness. Phosphorus in particular segregates to grain boundaries and readily causes embrittlement.

strengthening-015.question: Strengthening a metal usually reduces its uniform elongation. Which statement correctly describes the idea behind TRIP and TWIP steels, which show large uniform elongation even at high strength? Assume that necking begins when dσ/dε = σ (σ and ε are true stress and true strain).
choices: Martensitic transformation or deformation twinning during deformation keeps the work-hardening rate dσ/dε high as strain proceeds, delaying the onset of necking
Dislocations recover and disappear during deformation so that the work-hardening rate dσ/dε approaches zero, keeping the flow stress constant so that necking does not occur
Refining the grains to a few tens of nanometers raises the yield stress while keeping the work-hardening rate high, increasing strength and uniform elongation together
strengthening-015.explanation: By Considère's criterion, necking begins when the work-hardening rate dσ/dε has fallen to the flow stress σ. Raising σ by strengthening without raising the work-hardening rate reaches this condition sooner and reduces the uniform elongation. In TRIP steels retained austenite gradually transforms to hard martensite during deformation, and in TWIP steels deformation twins form one after another in high-Mn austenite with a low stacking-fault energy, with the twin boundaries finely dividing the paths of dislocations. In both, the work-hardening rate stays high as strain proceeds, so high strength and large uniform elongation are achieved together. If recovery brings the work-hardening rate close to zero, necking begins almost at once. In grains a few tens of nanometers in size, dislocations hardly accumulate within the grains, so the work-hardening rate falls and the uniform elongation becomes small.

strengthening-016.question: Carbon dissolved in ferrite (BCC iron) produces far more solid-solution strengthening per atom than substitutional solutes such as Mn. What is the main reason?
choices: Carbon atoms are larger than iron atoms, so they occupy lattice sites substitutionally and expand the surroundings strongly and spherically, attracting the hydrostatic stress field of edge dislocations
BCC octahedral sites have gaps that differ with direction, so carbon produces a tetragonal distortion that also interacts strongly with screw dislocations
When carbon atoms enter dislocation cores they form covalently bonded compounds with iron, fixing the dislocations permanently so that no stress can move them
strengthening-016.explanation: The octahedral site in BCC is a distorted gap: two iron atoms along one direction are close, while the four in the perpendicular plane are farther away. Carbon is much larger than this gap, so it pushes the two near iron atoms apart strongly and produces a tetragonal distortion biased in one direction. A spherically symmetric distortion has only a hydrostatic component and interacts mainly with edge dislocations, but a biased distortion also has a shear component, so it interacts strongly with all dislocations, including screw dislocations, and gives large strengthening. Carbon is an interstitial solute that sits between lattice sites, and it is smaller than an iron atom. Carbon collected at dislocations does pin them, but they can be torn away by sufficient stress, so they are not immobilized permanently.

strengthening-017.question: When Al-Mg alloys (such as the 5000 series) are pulled at room temperature, the stress–strain curve may rise and fall finely like the teeth of a saw, and band-like markings may appear on the surface (the Portevin–Le Chatelier effect). What is the cause?
choices: Deformation twins form one after another during deformation, and the stress drops suddenly each time a twin forms, so the curve rises and falls finely
With a testing machine of low stiffness the load oscillates for any alloy, so the curve rises and falls finely regardless of the material's properties
Solute atoms diffuse to and pin dislocations halted at obstacles, which are repeatedly torn free, so deformation localizes in bands
strengthening-017.explanation: During deformation, dislocations repeatedly halt at obstacles and then move on. In Al-Mg alloys at room temperature, Mg atoms diffuse to the dislocations during the short waiting time and pin them, so a larger stress is needed to move them. When the dislocations break free the stress drops, and they halt and are pinned again; this repetition is dynamic strain aging. Raising the strain rate shortens the time available for pinning and lowers the flow stress, giving a negative strain-rate sensitivity, so deformation localizes in propagating bands, the curve becomes serrated and markings are left on the surface. Blue brittleness in steel has the same mechanism. It is a phenomenon distinct from stress drops due to deformation twinning, and machine stiffness can affect the waveform but is not the cause itself.

strengthening-018.question: When a single crystal of an FCC metal such as copper is pulled in an orientation for single slip, the curve of resolved shear stress versus shear strain shows three stages. Which describes the stages correctly?
choices: Stage I is easy glide on a single slip system with little hardening, stage II has several systems active with a high, nearly constant hardening rate, and stage III shows a falling hardening rate due to dynamic recovery by cross-slip

Stage I has several slip systems active with the highest hardening rate, stage II has only one system active with a hardening rate of nearly zero, and stage III shows a stress drop due to recrystallization during deformation
The hardening rate is constant throughout the three stages, and the stages differ because the number of grain boundaries in the single crystal increases with strain
strengthening-018.explanation: In a single-slip orientation, dislocations at first travel long distances while hardly intersecting dislocations of other systems, giving easy glide with little hardening (stage I). When other slip systems start to operate, for example as the crystal rotates, dislocations of different systems intersect to form hard-to-move combinations, dislocations accumulate rapidly, and stage II follows with a nearly constant hardening rate of roughly the shear modulus divided by a few hundred. At higher stresses, screw dislocations avoid obstacles by cross-slip and annihilate dislocations of opposite sign, so the hardening rate gradually decreases in stage III. Stage III begins earlier at higher temperature and higher stacking-fault energy. A single crystal has no grain boundaries.

strengthening-019.question: The plastic shear strain rate is given by the Orowan equation γ̇ = ρm·b·v, using the density of mobile dislocations ρm, the magnitude of the Burgers vector b and the average dislocation velocity v. For deformation at γ̇ = 1.0×10⁻³ s⁻¹ with ρm = 1.0×10¹² m⁻² and b = 0.25 nm, which is closest to v?
choices: About 0.25 m/s
About 4 m/s
About 4 µm/s
strengthening-019.explanation: v = γ̇/(ρm·b) = 1.0×10⁻³/(1.0×10¹² × 0.25×10⁻⁹) = 4.0×10⁻⁶ m/s, or about 4 µm/s. About 0.25 m/s multiplies where it should divide, and its units would not even be m/s. About 4 m/s uses the square root √ρm = 1.0×10⁶ m⁻¹ instead of the dislocation density. Dislocation density is the dislocation length per unit volume (m/m³), and ρm·b·v corresponds to the area swept per unit time by dislocations on their slip planes times the amount of offset. At the strain rates of an ordinary tensile test, dislocations move far more slowly than sound (several km/s), advancing little by little on average while halting at obstacles. At the same strain rate, fewer mobile dislocations means each must move faster, which requires a larger stress.

strengthening-020.question: The Hall–Petch relation, in which the yield stress increases in proportion to the −1/2 power of the grain size d, is explained by dislocation pile-ups against grain boundaries. Which explanation is correct?
choices: The grain-boundary area increases in proportion to the square of the grain size, so the number of dislocation sources at boundaries increases and the yield stress increases in proportion to the square of the grain size
The head of a pile-up feels a stress amplified by the number of dislocations, which is proportional to grain size, so the external stress needed for slip in the next grain varies as 1/√d

The smaller the grains, the higher the dislocation density within them, increasing in proportion to the square root of the grain size, so by the Taylor equation the yield stress increases in proportion to √d
strengthening-020.explanation: Dislocations emitted from a source on a slip plane are stopped at the grain boundary and form a pile-up. The stress at the head of the pile-up is amplified to n times the external resolved shear stress τ, where n is the number of dislocations in the pile-up, and n is proportional to τ and to the pile-up length (proportional to the grain size). The head stress nτ is therefore proportional to τ²d, and the condition that it reaches the fixed value needed to operate a source in the next grain makes τ inversely proportional to √d; adding the friction stress gives σy = σ₀ + k/√d. Smaller grains mean shorter pile-ups and less amplification, so a larger external stress is required. Proportionality to the square of the grain size would make larger grains stronger, the wrong way round. Saying that dislocation density grows in proportion to √d as grains are refined also has the relation reversed.

strengthening-021.question: Which statement correctly explains, in terms of the lattice resistance to dislocation motion (the Peierls stress), why slip in many metals occurs most easily on close-packed planes in close-packed directions?
choices: The Peierls stress is smaller for small interplanar spacing and large Burgers vectors, and densely packed planes lie closest together, so dislocations move easily on them
It is smaller for wide plane spacing and small Burgers vectors; close-packed planes are the most widely spaced and close-packed directions give the shortest b
The Peierls stress is the same for all planes and directions, and slip systems are set not by crystal structure but only by specimen shape and loading direction
strengthening-021.explanation: In the Peierls–Nabarro model the Peierls stress is roughly proportional to exp[−2πd/((1 − ν)b)], falling exponentially as the slip-plane spacing d increases and the Burgers vector magnitude b decreases. The most densely packed planes are the most widely spaced, and along close-packed directions the distance to the next atom, that is, the shortest b, is available. Dislocations therefore move most easily on close-packed planes in close-packed directions, as in the {111}<110> slip of FCC. Saying that smaller spacing makes motion easier reverses the dependence. Slip systems are set by the crystal structure; the loading direction only decides which slip system operates first.

strengthening-022.question: Austenitic stainless steel (SUS304, equivalent to AISI 304) work-hardens more than aluminum during cold working and also has a larger uniform elongation before necking. Which explanation in terms of stacking-fault energy is correct?
choices: SUS304 has a low stacking-fault energy, so dislocations dissociate widely and cross-slip with difficulty; dynamic recovery is hindered and dislocations accumulate
SUS304 has a high stacking-fault energy, so dislocations dissociate narrowly and cross-slip easily, and the resulting dislocation multiplication gives strong hardening
Aluminum has a low stacking-fault energy, so dislocations dissociate widely and do not tangle with each other, which keeps its work hardening small
strengthening-022.explanation: SUS304 has a low stacking-fault energy, so dislocations split widely into two partial dislocations. Dissociated dislocations cannot easily bypass obstacles by cross-slip, so slip becomes planar and dynamic recovery, in which dislocations annihilate or rearrange, is suppressed. Dislocations keep accumulating, the work-hardening rate stays high, Considère's condition is reached later, and uniform elongation is larger (in SUS304, strain-induced martensite also contributes). Aluminum has a high stacking-fault energy and narrow dissociation, so cross-slip is easy, dynamic recovery proceeds, and work hardening is relatively small. Statements that swap the high and low stacking-fault energies of the two metals are wrong.

strengthening-023.question: When a dislocation gliding on its slip plane intersects another dislocation threading that plane (a forest dislocation), this contributes to work hardening. Which explanation is correct?
choices: On intersecting, the two dislocations merge into one and vanish, so fewer mobile dislocations remain and a higher stress is needed to continue deforming
On intersecting, a dislocation's Burgers vector grows by that of the other, raising its energy until it can no longer move
On intersecting, steps (jogs) form on the lines; a jog on a screw dislocation cannot glide with it and is dragged along, leaving point defects behind
strengthening-023.explanation: When two dislocations intersect, each line is offset by the other's Burgers vector, producing a step in the line. A step lying in the slip plane is called a kink, and one out of the slip plane a jog. A jog on a screw dislocation has edge character, and its glide plane does not match the direction the dislocation moves, so it cannot glide along; it is dragged by climb, leaving vacancies or interstitials behind. The higher the forest dislocation density, the larger the stress needed to move dislocations, which is part of the dislocation strengthening expressed by the Taylor equation. Intersection does not annihilate the dislocations, and the Burgers vector of a dislocation does not change on intersecting.

strengthening-024.question: Spherical precipitates of radius r are uniformly dispersed at volume fraction f. If each particle is taken to occupy a cube of edge L, the center-to-center spacing is L = [4πr³/(3f)]^(1/3). Which is closest to L for r = 5.0 nm and f = 0.050?
choices: About 22 nm
About 44 nm
About 4.7 nm
strengthening-024.explanation: The volume of one particle, (4/3)πr³, is the fraction f of the cube volume L³, so L³ = 4πr³/(3f). 4π × 5.0³/3 ≈ 524 nm³ divided by 0.050 is about 1.05×10⁴ nm³, and its cube root gives L ≈ 22 nm. About 44 nm uses the diameter of 10 nm instead of the radius, and about 4.7 nm substitutes the volume fraction as 5 (percent). The formula shows that at a fixed volume fraction the spacing is proportional to particle radius. Dispersing the same amount of precipitate more finely narrows the spacing and increases Orowan strengthening, Gb/L. This is also one reason strength falls when particles coarsen on overaging.

strengthening-025.question: Which is a characteristic of dual-phase (DP) steel, a ferrite–martensite steel used for car bodies and similar parts?
choices: Hard martensite is the matrix with small islands of ferrite dispersed in it, so the yield ratio is high and the steel is hard to press-form
Islands of hard martensite are dispersed in soft ferrite; there is no distinct yield point, the yield ratio is low and initial work hardening is high
Dislocations are pinned at the ferrite–martensite interfaces, so an even sharper yield point and Lüders bands appear than in annealed low-carbon steel
strengthening-025.explanation: DP steel is quenched from the two-phase ferrite + austenite range so that islands of hard martensite are dispersed in a soft ferrite matrix. The volume expansion of the martensite transformation introduces many mobile dislocations into the surrounding ferrite, so the steel yields smoothly without a yield-point phenomenon, with a fairly low yield stress and high tensile strength, that is, a low yield ratio. Work hardening is high from the start of deformation, so the steel press-forms well and the formed parts end up strong. Calling martensite the matrix reverses the roles of the phases. A sharp yield point contradicts this steel's key feature, its abundance of mobile dislocations.
